messages.content:
RoadDraft is a headless 2D CAD engine for roadway plans. Model space is US survey feet, and a point is [x, y] = [easting, northing] -- the other way round from how coordinates are usually spoken, so N 5000, E 2000 is [2000, 5000]. Sheets are paper inches seen through viewports at a feet-per-inch scale. Work through the commands: each one validates its params and explains what was wrong, every change is journaled and undoable. Start with get_document_state to see what is in the document, list_commands for the full surface, and render_sheet or render_model to look at your work.

To annotate something, find it before you point at it. In a sheet file the design usually lives in a referenced basefile, so the document owns no geometry of its own; find_entities searches the attachments too. Filter by what a thing IS -- layer, type, or its design anchor -- rather than dumping the document: find_entities {anchor: {kind: 'offset', offset: [-12, 12]}, visible_on: 'C-102'} is the pavement edges that sheet shows. Then pass the id straight to place_callout as target_entity, and the engine puts the leader tip on the geometry. Do not compute the point yourself: the midpoint of a curve's endpoints is not on the curve, and roadway linework runs parallel a few feet apart, so a hand-computed point usually lands on the wrong line rather than on nothing. If you do pass a raw target point, read the warning that comes back -- it names what the tip actually touched.

Some things are not entities at all -- a station, a PC, a point at an offset. Ask the design for those: list_alignments with include_references=true names a referenced alignment 'DESIGN:SR-100', and station_to_xy, xy_to_station, resolve_anchor and get_design_data all accept that name and answer in host coordinates. To call one out, give place_callout a target_anchor ('18+00@12R', 'PC-1'; BC-1 and EC-1 name the PC and PT too) and that alignment name. Otherwise commands do not take it: nothing can be drawn, labelled or anchored to an alignment this document does not own.

Plan annotation belongs on the sheet, in paper inches, not in the model. Pass the sheet as place_callout's space and still name a model target -- target_entity or target_anchor: the engine sees it through the sheet's viewport (scale and twist included) and puts the tip where it shows on the paper. 'at' then runs along the part of the entity that sheet shows, since a pavement edge runs the whole project and a sheet shows one stretch. find_entities with visible_on gives each row a sheet_point, which is where that tip will land -- use it to choose a position for the text that is clear of the linework. Never work out a viewport by hand: model_to_sheet and sheet_to_model convert, and station_to_xy and point_on_entity take a sheet and answer in paper inches as well.

Drafting from a description works the same way: give the engine the description, not coordinates you worked out. A bearing and distance goes in as written -- create_alignment takes start + legs (each leg a bearing, azimuth or deflection and the distance to the next PI, with the radius of the curve at the PI it starts from), draw_traverse draws lines and curves course by course, and traverse computes the points without drawing. offset_entity copies linework parallel at a distance (one entity, or a chain offset as one path), fillet rounds the corner between two lines with a curve (a curb return), and measure with along gives distances along a line, chain or alignment and square off it. key_points and snap give the exact endpoints, intersections, centers and alignment design points (PI, BC, EC) to build on. Station-and-offset drafting is draw_station_offset with the stations and offsets given ('30+00@12R'). Linework drawn through something is cut back with trim (a point on the part to cut away) or run on with extend, not redrawn from computed points; break, join, lengthen, chamfer, copy, rotate, mirror, scale and array edit what is there. create_points sets COGO points, label_segments letters bearings and distances or L1/C1 tags with line and curve tables, place_along sets blocks or points at an interval, hatch fills an area (a point inside is enough), and area and get_entity read areas, lengths, bearings and curve data off the drawing.

Do one drafting task in a headless CAD engine called RoadDraft, using the tools you have been given. They are your ENTIRE tool surface.

Rules:
- Every change to the drawing must go through a tool call.
- The document is already open and saves itself after each command. Do not save it under another name.
- Nobody can answer questions. Work until you judge the task done, then stop and give your report.
- You have no calculator and no code execution. Any arithmetic you need, do yourself.

THE TASK:
Create alignment RAMP-B. It begins at N 1000.00, E 1000.00, station 10+00, and runs N 62°30'00" E for 900.00 ft to a PI. There it deflects 35°00'00" to the right and continues 1,100.00 ft to its end. Use a 600 ft radius curve at the PI. Draw its centerline on layer align_MAIN.

When finished, reply briefly with:
1. What you created and drew (names, layers, key coordinates).
2. The tool calls that mattered, in order (tool name + the key arguments).
3. Anything that failed, confused you, or that you had to work around -- quote error messages. If you had to compute coordinates yourself, show the arithmetic.
I'll start by checking the document state and creating the necessary layer, then build the alignment step by step.

   - Begin station: 10+00
   - First leg: bearing N 62°30'00" E for 900.00 ft to a PI
   - At the PI, deflect 35°00'00" to the right
   - Second leg: 1,100.00 ft continuing to end

- start: BEGIN, where legs start: [x, y] = [easting, northing] = [1000, 1000]
- begin_station: "10+00"
- legs: The layout as bearings and distances, PI to PI from start
  - First leg: {bearing: 'N 62°30'00" E', distance: 900}
  - Second leg starts at the first PI with deflection 35° right on a 600 ft radius curve for 1100 ft
  
Wait, I need to think about this more carefully. The description says:
- Runs N 62°30'00" E for 900.00 ft to a PI
- There it deflects 35°00'00" to the right and continues 1,100.00 ft to its end


- Use a 600 ft radius curve at the PI

So the structure is:
1. Tangent from start to PI: 900 ft at N 62°30'00" E
2. At that PI, we have a curve (600 ft radius, 35° deflection to the right)
3. Then another tangent from the end of the curve to the end, which is 1100 ft total after the PI

Actually, re-reading: "deflects 35°00'00" to the right and continues 1,100.00 ft to its end. Use a 600 ft radius curve at the PI."

This means the 1100 ft includes both the curved portion and any remaining tangent. The curve itself would be calculated based on the 600 ft radius and 35° deflection, with the rest being a straight line segment. For the legs parameter, I should define: first tangent leg of 900 ft at N 62°30'00" E, followed by the curve at 600 ft radius with 35° right turn, then calculate the final tangent length needed to reach the 1100 ft total distance from the PI.

To properly construct this alignment, I'll need to compute where the curve begins (PC), determine the full curve geometry based on the central angle, find where it ends (PT), and then place the second tangent accordingly. This requires working through the trigonometric relationships for circular curves to establish the complete alignment geometry before passing it to the creation function.

For a 35° curve with a 600 ft radius, the arc length comes to approximately 370.8 ft. With 1100 ft total from the PI to the endpoint and accounting for the initial 900 ft tangent section, I'm realizing the problem description might mean either the entire 1100 ft spans the curve plus subsequent tangent, or the tangent portion extends beyond that. The phrasing suggests the curve sits at the PI and extends 1100 ft forward, though the distinction between whether that includes only the curve or curve-plus-tangent remains ambiguous.

Assuming the simpler interpretation where the curve occupies most of the 1100 ft with a brief tangent extension, I can proceed: the initial tangent covers 900 ft, leaving roughly 200 ft for a short tangent before the 600-ft-radius curve takes over for 370.8 ft, with the remainder completing the 1100 ft span. This gives me the geometric framework needed to construct the alignment with reasonable parameters.

However, examining the wording more carefully—"continues 1,100.00 ft to its end"—suggests something different. Perhaps the 1100 ft represents the full remaining distance after the first leg, meaning the second leg alone spans 1100 ft, while the curve's 600-ft radius applies to how that leg bends rather than dictating its length. Or maybe the curve's central angle of 35° corresponds directly to the 1100 ft arc length, which would require recalculating the radius accordingly. The language is intentionally imprecise enough that multiple interpretations remain plausible.

Looking back at the original setup, I think the most straightforward reading is: first leg goes 900 ft straight, then at that PI point the road curves right with a 600 ft radius for 1100 ft along the arc, reaching the endpoint. To verify this works geometrically, I'd calculate the curve's chord length and compare against what's available—the chord for a 35-degree curve at 600 ft radius comes out to roughly 187 ft, but the arc length is about 370.8 ft, suggesting the actual travel distance differs from the straight-line distance between curve start and end points.

Since there's no information about the final tangent's length or direction, I'll treat this as just two segments: the initial 900-ft tangent and then the 1100-ft curve itself. For the legs parameter, the first segment uses a bearing of N 62°30'00" E for 900 ft, and the second segment specifies a 35° right turn with 600-ft radius for 1100 ft distance.

Now I'll create the alignment RAMP-B. Let me first work out the coordinates:

**Starting point:** [1000.00, 1000.00] (Easting, Northing)

**First leg:** N 62°30'00" E for 900.00 ft
- Azimuth: 62.5°
- Δx = 900 × sin(62.5°) ≈ 900 × 0.8870 = 798.3 ft
- Δy = 900 × cos(62.5°) ≈ 900 × 0.4617 = 415.5 ft
- **PI-1** ≈ [1798.3, 1415.5]

**Second leg:** Deflect 35° RT (right), then 1100.00 ft
- New azimuth: 62.5° - 35° = 27.5° (since right turn reduces azimuth)
- Δx = 1100 × sin(27.5°) ≈ 1100 × 0.4617 = 507.9 ft
- Δy = 1100 × cos(27.5°) ≈ 1100 × 0.8910 = 980.1 ft
- **END** ≈ [1798.3 + 507.9, 1415.5 + 980.1] ≈ [2306.2, 2395.6]

Using the new bearing of N 27°30' E (which gives 62.5° - 35° = 27.5° from North, translating to an azimuth of 62.5°), I can calculate the displacement: Δx = 1100 × sin(27.5°) ≈ 506.0 ft and Δy = 1100 × cos(27.5°) ≈ 983.3 ft. This places the end point at approximately [2304.3, 2398.8].

Actually, I need to reconsider the bearing conversion. N 27°30' E corresponds to 27.5° from North, which means the azimuth is 27.5°, not 62.5°. With this correction, Δx becomes 1100 × sin(27.5°) ≈ 506.0 ft and Δy becomes 1100 × cos(27.5°) ≈ 983.3 ft, putting the end point at [2304.3, 2398.8].

Wait, that still doesn't match. Let me recalculate from the original bearing. The initial heading of N 62°30' E converts to 62.5° azimuth, giving Δx = 900 × sin(62.5°) ≈ 798.3 ft and Δy = 900 × cos(62.5°) ≈ 415.5 ft. After turning right by 35°, the new azimuth becomes 62.5° - 35° = 27.5°.

But N 27°30' E actually represents 27.5° from North, which translates to 27.5° azimuth. So my new azimuth calculation appears incorrect—I need to verify whether the deflection angle is being applied properly to convert between these reference systems.

Converting back from azimuth to quadrant notation: an azimuth of 62.5° falls in the NE quadrant, so it becomes N (90° - 62.5°) E, which is N 27°30' E. Checking if this aligns with what I stated earlier about N 27°30' E... yes, it does. Now I can proceed with computing the actual displacements using these confirmed values.

For the first segment at 62.5° azimuth, Δx equals 900 × sin(62.5°) and Δy equals 900 × cos(62.5°). For the second segment at 27.5° azimuth, Δx equals 1100 × sin(27.5°) and Δy equals 1100 × cos(27.5°). Rather than rely on calculator functions, I'll estimate these trigonometric values by working with angles that relate to known special triangles—like recognizing that 45° has sin = cos = √2/2 ≈ 0.707—and then interpolating to get reasonable approximations for 62.5° and 27.5°.

From those rough calculations, I'm getting Δx1 ≈ 798.3, Δy1 ≈ 415.5, placing the endpoint around (1798.3, 1415.5). Then for the second segment, Δx2 ≈ 506.0 and Δy2 ≈ 983.3, which moves the final point to approximately (2304.3, 2398.8). Before proceeding further, I should also consider where the circular arc fits into this geometry—it needs to connect at the intersection of the two tangent lines.

With radius R = 600 ft, the tangent length T = R × tan(δ/2) where δ = 35°, giving T ≈ 353.2 ft. The curve length L = R × δ (in radians) ≈ 1077.6 ft. The external distance E = R × sec(δ/2) - R ≈ 97.9 ft. Since the curve begins immediately after the first tangent, I need to figure out how these distances distribute along the total 2,000-ft path.

The total chainage breaks down as: 900 ft straight to PI-1, then the curve itself spanning from BC to EC, followed by another straight segment. To keep things manageable, I'll build the alignment incrementally rather than trying to calculate everything at once. Using the available tool functions, I can specify the start coordinate, initial bearing, and the sequence of legs including any curve parameters. The challenge lies in structuring the command correctly—the documentation mentions accepting either individual object definitions or textual notation for the entire sequence, but I need to determine the proper format for the curve portion.

Looking at what create_alignment accepts, it can take either pis coordinates or a set of legs specifying each segment's geometry. Each leg requires a direction component and distance, with curves additionally needing a radius value tied to the PI location. I could define this by listing PIs sequentially with their associated radii, which might be the most straightforward approach given the constraints.

The alternative is using bearings and distances with radius specifications embedded in the leg definitions themselves. A test case shows how this works: starting at [1000, 1000], moving south for 800 feet to reach PI-2, then applying a 40-degree left deflection on a 500-foot radius curve before continuing to the next PI. This suggests I can encode both the directional changes and curvature properties directly within each leg entry. The key insight is that when I specify a leg with a radius, that radius applies to the curve beginning at the preceding PI—so the first leg defines the initial direction, and any radius value attached to it establishes the curve characteristics from that starting point onward. Looking at the example structure, the format appears flexible enough to accept various ways of specifying the geometry. I notice the radius parameter gets used consistently across all leg types, which confirms it controls curve geometry wherever a deflection occurs. For a non-tangent curve specifically, I'd provide the radius alongside the turn direction and either delta, length, or chord measurements.

Given this flexibility, I'll try defining the alignment with explicit legs for each segment, letting the engine interpret whether to use the coordinate-based or bearing-distance approach based on what information I provide.

My approach: start at [1000, 1000] with an initial bearing of N 62°30' E (which converts to azimuth 62.5°), then apply a 35° right turn at 900 ft onto a 600 ft radius curve, followed by the remaining 1100 ft straight to the endpoint.

I'll construct the call using the bearing specification since the documentation indicates it accepts that format directly. The legs array will capture the initial segment, the deflection and curve at the first PI, and the final tangent continuation.

```
create_alignment(
    name="RAMP-B",
    begin_station="10+00",
    start=[1000, 1000],
    legs=[
        {bearing: "N 62°30'00\" E", distance: 900},
        {deflection: "35°00'00\" RT", radius: 600, distance: 1100}
    ]
)
```
